legal.headline: Delhi High Court seeks response from ED, SFIO on plea by Tina Ambani to disclose look out circular
legal.hook: Delhi High Court seeks response from ED, SFIO on plea by Tina Ambani to disclose look out circular

The petition argues that the LOCs impede her ability to travel abroad for personal reasons. The court’s order, dated 19 Oct 2024, references the Prevention of Money‑Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA) and the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA) as the statutory framework under which LOCs may be issued. No precedent directly on LOC disclosure was cited; the closest authority is the Supreme Court’s decision in *Union of India v. R. K. Sinha* (2022) on procedural fairness in enforcement actions, which the court noted but did not rely upon.

legal.summary: A New York court requested Patiala House Court, Dwarka Court and Tis Hazari Court to accept the summons cause them to be delivered on Doval and Samant Goel.

No Indian statute directly governs foreign courts’ requests for service, but the Indian Civil Procedure Code (CPC) Order II Rule 1 allows service of foreign judicial documents upon a court’s direction. No precedent exists where Indian courts have ordered service on a serving officer of the intelligence establishment.

legal.headline: Karnataka High Court quashes case against man who posted that Siddaramaiah will distribute nation's wealth to Muslims
legal.hook: Karnataka High Court quashes case against man who posted that Siddaramaiah will distribute nation's wealth to Muslims
legal.summary: The Court held that the social media post, even if taken at face value, did not satisfy the essential ingredients of Section 153A of IPC which criminalises promoting enmity between different groups on ground of religion.
legal.contextNote: Bar & Bench reports that the Karnataka High Court dismissed a criminal complaint under Section 153A of the Indian Penal Code for a social media post alleging that Karnataka Chief Minister Siddaramaiah would "distribute the nation's wealth to Muslims." The bench held the post, even on its face, did not contain the requisite intent or likelihood of inciting communal hatred, thus failing the essential ingredients of Section 153A IPC. No other statutes or precedents were cited; the decision rests on established jurisprudence that the provision requires a clear act of promoting enmity, not merely a provocative statement.
